stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The application keeps no state on the instances, and users reach it through one DNS name. After several short outages, the company wants a more reliable design. The application must remain available if an Availability Zone fails. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Run the instances in two Availability Zones of the current Region behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones.
options.why: Two zones meet the requirement, and the reliability pillar asks for production workloads in [at least two Availability Zones (AZs) in a Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-production-at-least-two-azs).

options.text: Run a second copy of the application in another AWS Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing with health checks to send users to the healthy copy.
options.why: It also survives a zone failure, but it pays for a full copy in a second Region, and [most customers can achieve their resilience goals in a single Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-most-customers-single-region-suffices).

options.text: Run active copies of the application in three AWS Regions at the same time, and use Amazon Route 53 latency routing with health checks to send each user to a copy.
options.why: Three active Regions survive a zone failure, but AWS names this anti-pattern: [you implement a multi-Region architecture when a multi-AZ architecture would satisfy business requirements](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-when-multi-az-suffices-is-anti-pattern).

options.text: Add more instances in the current Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that replaces any unhealthy instance.
options.why: If all instances are in one zone and that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), however many instances run there.

explanation: An EC2 instance is a zonal resource, [specific to the Availability Zone in which you create it](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-zonal-resource-deploy-in-multiple-azs). AWS says to [deploy your application in multiple Availability Zones, so that your application remains available even if one Availability Zone fails](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-zonal-resource-deploy-in-multiple-azs). A second zone in the same Region adds a few instances and a load balancer, which costs less than a copy in another Region.
takeaway: A zone failure calls for two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, not a second Region.
twin: If the stem said "must remain available if the AWS Region fails" instead: the second copy in another Region, because the separation between Regions [avoids correlated failures between them](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-avoids-correlated-failures).
say: Two Availability Zones behind a load balancer survive a zone failure, and that is the cheapest fix.

stem: A company runs an order-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company chose the Linux operating system of the instances when it launched them. A new security engineer reviews the AWS shared responsibility model to plan the work of the security team. A vendor publishes a security patch for a vulnerability in that Linux operating system. Which task is the responsibility of the company?
keywords: a security patch for a vulnerability in that Linux operating system

options.text: Apply security patches to the virtualization layer of the physical hosts that run the EC2 instances.
options.why: AWS controls the components [from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-aws-controls-host-os-virtualization-and-facilities).
options.misconception: The customer patches the virtualization layer under its EC2 instances.

options.text: Control physical access to the data center facilities that hold the hosts that run the EC2 instances.
options.why: Facilities are part of the infrastructure, and AWS protects [the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS Cloud services](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-aws-responsible-for-infrastructure-security-of-the-cloud).
options.misconception: The customer secures the data center buildings that run its instances.

options.text: Apply the security patch to the guest operating system that runs on each of the EC2 instances.
options.why: Patch management is shared, and [customers are responsible for patching their guest OS and applications](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control).

options.text: Ask AWS to apply the security patch to the guest operating system in the next maintenance window.
options.why: EC2 is [categorized as Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-ec2-is-iaas-customer-does-all-security-configuration), so AWS does not patch the guest operating system for the company.

explanation: Patch management is a shared control. [AWS is responsible for patching and fixing flaws within the infrastructure](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control), and [customers are responsible for patching their guest OS and applications](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control). The company chose the operating system on its instances, so the company applies the patch.
takeaway: On EC2, AWS patches the infrastructure and the customer patches the guest operating system.
twin: If the stem said "tables in Amazon DynamoDB" instead: AWS applies the patches, because for multi-tenant managed services AWS will [apply patches without requiring customer action](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-multi-tenant-managed-services-aws-patches-without-customer-action).
say: On EC2 you patch the guest operating system; AWS patches the hosts and the virtualization layer below it.

stem: A company stores sensitive customer contracts as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company keeps the metadata of each contract as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table. An auditor asks the company to list the security tasks that the company owns for these two services under the AWS shared responsibility model. Which tasks are the responsibility of the company? (Select TWO.)
keywords: the security tasks that the company owns

options.text: Apply operating system patches to the hosts that run the Amazon S3 service and the Amazon DynamoDB service.
options.why: For abstracted services such as these, [AWS operates the infrastructure layer, the operating system, and platforms](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-abstracted-services-aws-runs-os-customer-manages-data).
options.misconception: The customer patches the operating system under a managed service.

options.text: Write IAM policies that give each application and each user the access that it needs to the bucket and the table.
options.why: The customer is responsible for [managing their data (including encryption options), classifying their assets, and using IAM tools to apply the appropriate permissions](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-abstracted-services-aws-runs-os-customer-manages-data).

options.text: Replace failed disks and maintain the storage hardware that holds the objects in the bucket and the items in the table.
options.why: Storage hardware is infrastructure, and AWS protects [the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS Cloud services](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-aws-responsible-for-infrastructure-security-of-the-cloud).
options.misconception: The customer maintains the hardware under a managed storage service.

options.text: Choose and configure the encryption options for the objects in the bucket and for the items in the table.
options.why: The data and its protection stay with the company, because [you retain control of the security you choose to implement](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-security-in-the-cloud-you-retain-control).

options.text: Let AWS decide which users and applications can read the objects and the items, because AWS manages both services.
options.why: Access to the data is security in the cloud: [while AWS manages security of the cloud, you are responsible for security in the cloud](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-security-in-the-cloud-you-retain-control).

explanation: Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB are abstracted services. [AWS operates the infrastructure layer, the operating system, and platforms](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-abstracted-services-aws-runs-os-customer-manages-data). The company still owns its data, the encryption options of that data, and the IAM permissions that decide who can reach it.
takeaway: On S3 and DynamoDB, AWS runs the platform, and the customer owns permissions and encryption choices.
twin: If the stem said "Amazon EC2 instances" instead: guest operating system patches join the list, because [customers are responsible for patching their guest OS and applications](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control).
say: On S3 and DynamoDB, AWS runs the platform; you own who can read the data and how it is encrypted.

stem: A company runs an interactive design application on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Most users work in one large city that is far from every AWS Region. The application processes each user action in real time, and the users report slow responses. The company wants to run the EC2 instances closer to users and needs single-digit millisecond latency for them. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for these users?
keywords: one large city that is far from every AWS Region

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the Regional EC2 instances as the origin, so that users connect to an edge location.
options.why: Points of presence host [Amazon CloudFront](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-pop-hosts-cloudfront-route53-global-accelerator), but each user action is still processed on the instances in the distant Region.

options.text: Move the EC2 instances to the AWS Region that is nearest to the city, and keep the current Region as a warm standby.
options.why: It lowers latency, but the nearest Region is still far from the city, while Local Zones sit [close to large population and industry centers](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zones-definition-close-to-population-centers).

options.text: Move the application to larger EC2 instance types with more vCPUs in the current Region to process each action faster.
options.why: Larger instances shorten the processing time, but the network distance between the city and the Region stays the same.
options.misconception: Larger instances fix the delay that network distance causes.

options.text: Enable a Local Zone near the city, create a subnet in that Local Zone, and run the EC2 instances in that subnet.
options.why: To use a Local Zone, [you must first enable it](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zone-must-be-enabled-then-subnet), then [create a subnet in the Local Zone](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zone-must-be-enabled-then-subnet) and launch the instances there.

explanation: Local Zones are designed for workloads that need [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-single-digit-millisecond-latency-workloads). A Local Zone is [an extension of an AWS Region in geographic proximity to your users](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zone-extension-of-region-own-internet), so the EC2 instances run near the city instead of in a distant Region.
takeaway: Compute near the users of one city runs in a Local Zone; CloudFront at the edge does not move the compute.
twin: If the stem said "users connect from 5G mobile devices on one carrier network" instead: AWS Wavelength, because it is designed for [ultralow-latency applications to 5G devices](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-wavelength-ultralow-latency-for-5g-devices).
say: For compute near one city, I'd use a Local Zone; an edge location runs CloudFront, not your instances.

stem: A company stores product images in one Amazon S3 bucket in a single AWS Region. A web application in the same Region shows the images to users around the world. Users far from the Region report that pages load slowly because the images take a long time to download. The images change once a week, and the application itself responds fast. Which solution will improve the download times for these users with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the images take a long time to download

options.text: Copy the S3 bucket and the web application to several AWS Regions, and route each user to the nearest Region with Amazon Route 53 latency routing.
options.why: It works, but in a multi-Region design [you must duplicate your workload's components in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-duplicate-everything-no-cross-region-dependency), which adds far more operational work.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and serve the images to the users through the distribution.
options.why: One distribution in front of the existing bucket puts the images at edge locations near the users, and the bucket and the application stay as they are.

options.text: Enable a Local Zone in each city where users report slow pages, and run copies of the application and the image storage there.
options.why: Local Zones bring [the core services needed for the latency-sensitive portions of your workload](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-vs-availability-zones-core-vs-full-services) close to users, but a copy in every city adds much more work.
options.misconception: A Local Zone is the AWS tool for global content delivery.

options.text: Move the images to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access storage class, and turn on S3 Versioning to keep each weekly change.
options.why: The images still download from the one Region, so the distance to the users and the slow pages stay the same.
options.misconception: The S3 storage class changes the download speed for distant users.

explanation: [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, AWS Firewall Manager, AWS Shield, and AWS WAF services are provided through AWS Edge Locations](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-edge-location-services). A CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket serves the images from edge locations near the users. The bucket, the Region and the application do not change.
takeaway: Static content for users around the world: put CloudFront in front of the bucket.
twin: If the stem said "users in one city run an interactive application on EC2" instead: a Local Zone, because it suits workloads that need [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-single-digit-millisecond-latency-workloads).
say: For static files and users everywhere, put CloudFront in front of the bucket and keep one Region.

stem: A company runs its production workload on Amazon EC2 instances in the Asia Pacific (Sydney) Region to serve users in Australia. The engineers also work in Sydney. The company needs a new development and test environment that holds only synthetic test data. The company has no data privacy, security, or business requirements about where the environment runs, and extra latency for the engineers is not a concern. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: no data privacy, security, or business requirements

options.text: Run the development and test EC2 instances in the Asia Pacific (Sydney) Region, next to the production workload of the company.
options.why: It works, but resource prices are [different in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-pricing-differs-local-market), and nothing in the stem requires Sydney.

options.text: Run the development and test EC2 instances in a Local Zone near the office of the engineers to give them lower latency.
options.why: The stem says latency is not a concern, and resources in Local Zones have [different prices than they do in parent AWS Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zones-pricing-no-enable-charge-different-prices).
options.misconception: A Local Zone is a cheaper place to run test workloads.

options.text: Run the development and test EC2 instances in a Region with lower prices than Sydney, such as US East (N. Virginia).
options.why: AWS gives this case as its own example: [deploying non-critical (development and test) Amazon EC2 instances in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1) will cost you less](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-cheaper-region-for-non-critical-when-no-restrictions).

options.text: Run the development and test EC2 instances on AWS Outposts in the office of the company, so that the test data stays on premises.
options.why: Outposts is for [workloads that need to remain on premises due to latency requirements](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-outposts-for-workloads-that-must-stay-on-premises), and this test environment has no such requirement.

explanation: AWS says to [use Regions that provide lower prices for AWS services to deploy your workloads if you have no obligations in data privacy, security and business requirements](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-cheaper-region-for-non-critical-when-no-restrictions). The stem removes each of those obligations and says latency is not a concern, so price decides the Region.
takeaway: With no residency, security, or latency need, choose the lower-priced Region for development and test.
twin: If the stem said "the test data includes customer records that must stay in Australia" instead: the Sydney Region, because AWS says to [only deploy in Regions with higher costs to meet latency, data residency and data sovereignty requirements](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-region-pricing-differs-choose-by-cost).
say: Prices differ by Region, so with no data rules I'd put development and test in a cheaper Region.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The application keeps no state on the instances, and users reach it through one DNS name. After several short outages, the company wants a more reliable design. The application must remain available if the AWS Region fails. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Run the instances in two Availability Zones of the current Region behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones.
options.why: Two zones survive a zone failure, but both zones sit inside the failed Region, so the application stops with that Region.

options.text: Run a second copy of the application in another AWS Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing with health checks to send users to the healthy copy.
options.why: A copy in a second Region does not share the failure, and Route 53 can [use the status of health checks to perform failovers between Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-route53-failover-use-health-checks-not-record-changes).

options.text: Run active copies of the application in three AWS Regions at the same time, and use Amazon Route 53 latency routing with health checks to send each user to a copy.
options.why: Three active Regions also survive the failure, but they run three full copies where one copy in a second Region meets the requirement.

options.text: Add more instances in the current Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that replaces any unhealthy instance.
options.why: If that one zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), and a Region failure takes that zone too.

explanation: Each Region is [designed to be isolated from the other Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance), and that separation [avoids correlated failures between them](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-avoids-correlated-failures). A copy in a second Region keeps serving when the first Region fails, and Route 53 health checks send users to it. One standby copy costs less than active copies in three Regions.
takeaway: A Region failure needs a copy in a second Region; the zones of the failed Region fail with it.
twin: If the stem said "must remain available if an Availability Zone fails" instead: two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, because [most customers can achieve their resilience goals in a single Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-most-customers-single-region-suffices).
say: To survive a Region failure, you need a second copy in another Region and health-check failover.

stem: A company is expanding into a new country where an AWS Region exists. A new law requires that the personal data of customers in that country must remain in the country. The company will store the data in Amazon S3 and process it on Amazon EC2 instances. Other AWS Regions nearby offer lower prices. Which solution will ensure data residency with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create the S3 bucket and the EC2 instances in the Region in that country, and do not turn on any cross-Region replication or copy feature.
options.why: AWS services [process and store customer content in the AWS region(s) where the services are used by the customer](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-customer-content-stays-in-chosen-region), so the data stays in that country.

options.text: Create the resources in the Region in that country, and turn off the account setting that lets AWS copy data to other Regions.
options.why: There is nothing to turn off: AWS keeps resources out of other Regions [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).

options.text: Create the resources in a lower-priced Region in a neighboring country, because that Region is the nearest one with lower prices.
options.why: The services [process and store customer content in the AWS region(s) where the services are used by the customer](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-customer-content-stays-in-chosen-region), so the data would sit in the other country.
options.misconception: A nearby Region in another country satisfies a data residency law.

options.text: Create the resources in the Region in that country, and run a scheduled job that deletes any copies of the data in other Regions.
options.why: The job adds work with no effect, because no copy exists in another Region [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).

explanation: AWS services [process and store customer content in the AWS region(s) where the services are used by the customer](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-customer-content-stays-in-chosen-region). So the data stays in the Region in that country as long as the company adds no replication or copy feature. No extra setting or job is needed.
takeaway: Data stays in the Region you choose unless you configure replication or copying yourself.
twin: If the stem said "the law allows any Region inside the European Union" instead: the lowest-priced Region in the European Union, because prices are [different in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-pricing-differs-local-market).
say: Your data stays in the Region you pick; nothing leaves it unless you turn on replication or copy it.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that will ensure data residency with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the personal data must remain in one country, that country has an AWS Region, and the data lives in Amazon S3 and on EC2 instances. The lower prices nearby are bait.
Before I look at the options, I predict: create everything in the Region in that country and add no replication, because AWS stores customer content in the Region where I use the service.

I remove the neighboring Region, because the data would sit in another country. I remove the account setting, because there is no such setting: AWS does not copy my data to another Region unless I use a replication or copy feature.

Between the plain deployment and the deployment with a cleanup job, the difference is extra work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, and the job deletes copies that do not exist, so I choose the plain deployment.
Check: the Region in that country with no replication meets the law, needs no job, and needs no setting. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs a managed relational database for an order system in one AWS Region. The database must lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails. If the whole Region fails, the company must be able to recover the database in a second Region, and a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails
a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable

options.text: Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with synchronous replication from the primary database.
options.why: The zones of a Region are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms), so the standby holds every committed write.

options.text: Keep a replica of the database in a second AWS Region, with synchronous replication so that a Region failover loses no write.
options.why: AWS [does not provide a synchronous Cross-Region replication feature](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-synchronous-cross-region-replication), so this replica cannot be built with an AWS feature.

options.text: Keep a replica of the database in a second AWS Region, with asynchronous replication from the primary database in the first Region.
options.why: The Region copy is asynchronous, and the stem accepts [the possibility of data loss or inconsistency when you fail over](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-async-cross-region-replication-may-lose-data) of a few minutes.

options.text: Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with asynchronous replication every few minutes.
options.why: Asynchronous replication can leave the newest writes behind, so a zone failure can lose committed writes that the stem does not allow.
options.misconception: Any copy in a second zone protects every committed write.

options.text: Run a self-managed database on EC2 instances in a second AWS Region, and write a custom process that ships the changes every minute.
options.why: It can meet the few minutes of loss, but a self-managed database and a custom process add far more operational work than a managed replica.

explanation: The two failures need two kinds of copy. Inside the Region, the zones are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms). Between Regions, AWS [does not provide a synchronous Cross-Region replication feature](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-synchronous-cross-region-replication), so the Region copy is asynchronous.
takeaway: Synchronous copies work between zones; copies between Regions are asynchronous and can lose recent writes.
twin: If the stem said "a Region failure must lose no committed write" instead: no AWS replication feature meets it, because AWS [does not provide a synchronous Cross-Region replication feature](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-synchronous-cross-region-replication).
say: Synchronous to a second zone for zero loss, asynchronous to a second Region with a few minutes of loss.

stem: A company runs a latency-sensitive application in AWS account A and its database in AWS account B, in the same AWS Region. The VPCs of the two accounts are connected, and each account creates subnets in its own VPC. The company wants the application instances and the database in the same physical Availability Zone. The engineers in each account choose zones by the names that their own console shows, such as us-east-1a. The company must ensure that both workloads use the same physical zone. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: choose zones by the names that their own console shows
ensure that both workloads use the same physical zone

options.text: Create the application subnet in the zone that has the same Availability Zone name, such as us-east-1a, as the database subnet in the other account.
options.why: A zone name [might not be the same physical location as it is in another account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-name-mapping-independent-per-account), so matching names does not ensure one physical zone.
options.misconception: An Availability Zone name such as us-east-1a is the same physical zone in every account.

options.text: Move the application and the database into one AWS account, so that both workloads see the same zone names for the same physical zones.
options.why: It can work, but moving a workload between accounts is far more work than reading one zone attribute in each account.

options.text: Open an AWS Support case to ask AWS to map the Availability Zone names of both accounts to the same physical zones.
options.why: No support case is needed, because an AZ ID already names [the same physical location in every AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-id-same-physical-location-every-account).
options.misconception: AWS Support remaps the zone names of an account on request.

options.text: Look up the AZ ID of the database subnet, such as use1-az2, and create the application subnet in the zone with the same AZ ID.
options.why: An AZ ID names [the same physical location in every AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-id-same-physical-location-every-account), so equal AZ IDs mean one physical zone.

explanation: An Availability Zone ID (AZ ID) names [the same physical location in every AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-id-same-physical-location-every-account). Each team looks up the AZ ID of the database zone and creates its subnet in the zone with the matching AZ ID. This needs no move between accounts and no support case.
takeaway: Across accounts, match Availability Zones by AZ ID, not by zone name.
twin: If the stem said "both workloads run in one AWS account" instead: the zone name is enough, because one account sees one physical zone behind each of its zone names.
say: Across accounts I'd match zones by AZ ID, because the AZ ID is the same physical zone everywhere.

stem: An engineer at a company launched three Amazon EC2 instances yesterday by using the AWS Management Console. Today the engineer signs in to the console again and opens the list of EC2 instances. The list is empty. Nobody in the company stopped, terminated, or moved any instance, and the IAM permissions of the engineer are unchanged. What is the most likely reason for the empty list?
keywords: Nobody in the company stopped, terminated, or moved any instance

options.text: AWS moved the instances to another AWS Region overnight to balance the capacity of its data centers.
options.why: AWS does not move the instances, because a regional resource is [specific to the Region in which you create it](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-regional-resource-visible-only-in-its-region).

options.text: The console is showing a different AWS Region from the Region where the engineer launched the instances.
options.why: When created resources do not appear, [the console might be displaying resources from a different Region](../facts/management-console.md#management-console-missing-resources-check-region).

options.text: The instances stopped overnight, and the EC2 console hides stopped instances from the list of instances.
options.why: The stem says that no instance was stopped, so a hidden stopped instance does not explain the empty list.
options.misconception: The EC2 console hides stopped instances.

options.text: The EC2 console lists the instances of an account only when the engineer signs in from the same computer.
options.why: The list follows the selected Region, and [you see only the resources that are tied to that Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-regional-resource-visible-only-in-its-region).
options.misconception: The console view depends on the device that the engineer uses.

explanation: EC2 instances are regional resources: [Some resources (such as Amazon EC2 instances) are specific to the Region where they were created](../facts/management-console.md#management-console-missing-resources-check-region). The console shows one Region at a time, and [you see only the resources that are tied to that Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-regional-resource-visible-only-in-its-region). The engineer selects the launch Region, and the instances appear.
takeaway: Instances missing from the console: check the selected Region first.
twin: If the stem said "created an IAM role yesterday" instead: the Region is not the cause, because [You don't need to choose a Region for the AWS Management Console or for some services, such as AWS Identity and Access Management](../facts/management-console.md#management-console-some-services-need-no-region-selection).
say: If your instances seem gone, check the Region selector first; EC2 instances live in one Region.

stem: A company runs a mission-critical web tier on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The Region has three Availability Zones. Load tests show that the tier needs six instances to serve peak traffic. The tier must keep full peak capacity during the failure of one Availability Zone. Which design will meet these requirements and be the MOST resilient?
keywords: needs six instances to serve peak traffic
keep full peak capacity during the failure of one Availability Zone

options.text: Run nine instances, three in each Availability Zone, so that the two remaining zones still hold six running instances after one zone fails.
options.why: The spare capacity already runs, and [having that extra capacity pre-provisioned helps achieve static stability](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-pre-provision-capacity-instead-of-control-plane-recovery).

options.text: Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, and let the Auto Scaling group launch replacement instances in the other zones after a zone failure.
options.why: Replacements come late, because [launching new EC2 instances takes time](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-auto-scaling-relies-on-ec2-control-plane) and [deploying new instances through auto scaling relies on the EC2 control plane](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-auto-scaling-relies-on-ec2-control-plane).
options.misconception: Auto Scaling replaces the capacity of a failed Availability Zone at once, so pre-provisioned spare capacity is waste.

options.text: Run six instances in the Availability Zone with the most free capacity, and let the Auto Scaling group replace any unhealthy instance in that zone.
options.why: If that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), so the tier loses all of its capacity.

options.text: Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, and keep a copy of the tier with no running instances in a second AWS Region.
options.why: A standby Region answers a Region failure; during a zone failure, the tier runs on four instances until new instances launch.

explanation: A statically stable design can [continue to operate as normal without the need to make changes during the failure or unavailability of dependencies](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-static-stability-definition). The AWS example deploys [three instances in each Availability Zone, for a total of nine](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-static-stability-example-three-per-az-fifty-percent), so a zone failure leaves the full capacity running.
takeaway: To keep full capacity through a zone failure, pre-provision the spare capacity in the other zones.
twin: If the stem said "can run at reduced capacity for an hour after a zone failure" instead: six instances across three zones with Auto Scaling, because the tier can wait while replacements launch.
say: Pre-provision the spare capacity in every zone, so a zone failure needs no new launches.
